title: Two permutations with equal characteristic value admit representatives meeting exactly in the certificates
source_title: Uniqueness for 2-Intersecting Families of Permutations and Perfect Matchings

standard_prerequisites.name: 2-intersecting family of permutations
standard_prerequisites.statement: A family of permutations such that any two of its members agree in at least two positions.
standard_prerequisites.use: Its characteristic function is the object of the statement.

standard_prerequisites.name: Certificate of a permutation
standard_prerequisites.statement: The set of pairs on which a permutation is fixed, used to name the members of the family by a common core.
standard_prerequisites.use: They are the sets whose intersection is prescribed in the conclusion.

standard_prerequisites.name: C(f)
standard_prerequisites.statement: The smallest size of a certificate common to the family's members, bounded in the hypothesis.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the bound that makes the construction possible.

core_obligations: Aim at the stronger statement that representatives can be chosen so that their certificates meet exactly in the intersection of the two given certificates (source line 246).

Construct the first representative by listing the pairs of its certificate and then pairing the remaining indices cyclically, arranged so that no new pair meets the second certificate (source lines 248-254).
Repeat the construction with the two certificates exchanged, which is possible because the hypothesis is symmetric in the two members (source line 256).

proof_roadmap.step: Set up the stronger statement and list the pairs of the first certificate.
Pair the free indices cyclically so the new pairs avoid the other certificate.
Exchange the roles to build the second representative.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 242-244: for a 2-intersecting family of permutations whose common certificate size is at most n minus two, two members with equal characteristic value admit representatives whose certificates meet exactly in the intersection of the original certificates. The proof (source lines 245-257) proves the stronger statement about the intersection rather than merely about the characteristic values, and its heart is a pairing argument: after listing the pairs of the first certificate, the remaining indices are paired cyclically in an order chosen so that none of the new pairs meets the second certificate, which is exactly where the bound on the common certificate size is consumed; the same construction is then run with the certificates exchanged. The statement records only the existence of the representatives.
